title: Nanak at Baghdad
hook: Nanak and Mardana at Baghdad, where he speaks of worlds beyond worlds (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mecca, and your line, deeds, not labels. Did you do one good thing with no name on it? Day seven hundred three.

Two travelers have stopped at a great city. One is Baba Nanak. The other carries a rebab, a stringed instrument, and his name is Mardana. The city is Baghdad, and the var puts their camp outside it, beyond the walls. Bhai Gurdas sets the scene in a single line: here is Baba, and here is Mardana, the rebab player. Then something happens that makes everything go quiet. Today: karah prashad.
screen: `CAMP OUTSIDE A GREAT CITY.` → `BABA, AND MARDANA WITH HIS REBAB.` → `EVERYTHING GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak gave a call, and the world around fell silent, as if in a trance. A holy man of the city, a pir, came to see who this faqir was. And somewhere in the talk that followed, Nanak spoke of what lies beyond the edges of the known world: skies beyond skies, and worlds below worlds, past anyone's counting. The pir asked to be shown. And in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak took the pir's son with him, and in the blink of an eye showed him those worlds, and they came back carrying a bowl of karah prashad, the sweet offering, from a world below. You can hold that last part however your tradition holds it. Some readers take it as it's told. Others hear it as a picture. Either way, the story is about size. If you learned the Japji in year one, you've heard this before, in the Guru's own words. In the twenty-second pauri, Guru Nanak says there are nether worlds below nether worlds, and skies above skies. People have tried to find the limit, and they can't. If it could be written down, someone would write it, but the writing would run out first. That's the thread. The pir's world had edges. Nanak's answer took the edges away. Not to make anyone feel small, but to make God large: whatever you've counted, the Creator is beyond it. And notice who is in the scene's first line. Bhai Gurdas names two people at that camp: Baba, and Mardana, the rebab player. Even a story about countless worlds starts with a musician sitting beside his friend outside the walls.
screen: `A CALL, AND THE CITY FALLS SILENT.` · `SKIES BEYOND SKIES, WORLDS BELOW WORLDS.` · `THE JAPJI, PAURI 22: PAST COUNTING.` · `STILL, THE FRIEND AT YOUR SIDE.` · then, large: `WORLDS BEYOND WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at the night sky. If it's dark where you are, go outside or to a window and look up. Find the farthest light you can see, and then remember that it's not the edge. If it's daytime, close your eyes and picture the sky over your roof at midnight, and the dark behind the stars. Either way, let your breath slow down under all that size. You don't have to understand any of it. Just let it be bigger than you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, wonder, to the dark. The bell holds the time.
Karah prashad, the sweet offering Nanak and the pir's son brought back from a world below, in Bhai Gurdas's telling of worlds beyond counting.
Your line: worlds beyond worlds. Tonight, before sleep, look up once, through a window or in your mind, and let the day's worries be the size they really are. Day seven hundred three.

howItsDone: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's visit to Baghdad from Bhai Gurdas's first var, and connect his words there to the Japji's teaching that creation has no limit anyone can count.

fork.reveal: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak speaks of worlds beyond worlds, as the Japji does: if it could be written down, the writing would run out first.

what it means: Nanak takes the edges off the known world, to make God large rather than anyone small.
what a scholar hears: the scene in Bhai Gurdas echoes the Japji's pauri 22, where even the writing of the count runs out.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauris 35–36 (Nanak and Mardana at Baghdad)

notes: Var 1 pauris 35–36 paraphrased from memory: Nanak camps outside Baghdad with Mardana; gives a call (ditee baang) and the world falls silent; the pir (Dastgir) asks who this faqir is; Nanak speaks of countless skies and nether worlds; he takes the pir's son and in a blink shows him the worlds, returning with a bowl of karah prashad. Confirm pauri numbers and every detail, especially the karah prashad and whether the call is fairly rendered as 'a call'.
The var's 'lakh' (hundreds of thousands) is rendered 'past anyone's counting' to avoid stating a number.
The miraculous journey is framed as 'in Bhai Gurdas's telling', with 'some readers take it as it's told, others hear it as a picture'. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with this.
Mardana 'walked beside Nanak for years': year 1 day 31 calls him a lifelong companion; confirm.

Editor (claims rule): cut unsourced 'old man whose fame has run ahead' and 'walked beside Nanak for years'; 'the whole city' made 'everything' to match the var's 'the world fell silent'; hook adds that they camp outside Baghdad, as the var says.

Audit (day 703): cut the unsourced 'neither of them goes in' (the var says only that they camped outside); replaced the vague 'look at what it's carrying' and the closing uplift ('the friend at your side') with the concrete detail of Mardana named in the opening line.
